Phonetics is the scientific study of the sounds that humans produce when they speak.

Notice the word "sounds" here — not words, not grammar, not meaning — just the raw, physical sounds that come out of your mouth when you talk. That is the entire focus of phonetics.

When you speak, your body does something quite complex. Your lungs push air out, your vocal cords vibrate (or don't), your tongue moves to different positions, your lips open and close, and your teeth and the roof of your mouth all play a role — and the result is a stream of sounds. Phonetics is the field that examines all of this in careful detail.

It asks questions like:

  • How is a particular sound physically made inside the mouth and throat?
  • What does that sound look like as a sound wave travelling through the air?
  • How does the human ear and brain receive and recognise that sound?

These three questions give phonetics its three main branches (more on those below).

1. Articulatory Phonetics

This branch studies how speech sounds are physically produced — that is, how your body's "articulators" (tongue, lips, teeth, jaw, vocal cords, etc.) move and work together to create each sound.

For example: when you say the sound "p" (as in pen), you press your two lips together, build up a little air pressure behind them, and then release it in a small burst. Articulatory phonetics would describe exactly that — where the lips meet, what the airstream does, whether or not the vocal cords vibrate (for "p," they don't — but for "b" they do, which is why "p" and "b" feel so similar yet sound different).

This is probably the most widely studied branch, because understanding how sounds are made helps in many practical areas like language teaching, treating speech disorders, and designing voice-recognition technology.

2. Acoustic Phonetics

Once a sound leaves your mouth, it travels through the air as a sound wave. Acoustic phonetics studies the physical properties of those sound waves — their frequency (how high or low the pitch is), their amplitude (how loud or soft), and their duration (how long they last).

This branch uses scientific instruments to measure and visually display speech sounds. A tool called a spectrogram turns a spoken word into a visual graph, and acoustic phoneticians can "read" that graph to identify which sounds were spoken, how they behaved, and how they differ from one language or speaker to another.

3. Auditory (or Perceptual) Phonetics

This branch studies the listener's side of speech — how the human ear receives sound waves and how the brain processes and interprets them as recognisable speech sounds.

It asks: why do you hear a "b" and not a "p" even when the two sounds are physically very close? How do you understand someone through noise, a thick accent, or a phone call with bad signal? These are auditory phonetics questions.
An important distinction: Phonetics vs. Phonology

These two words are often confused, so it is worth being clear.

Phonetics is concerned with the physical, concrete sounds themselves — how they are made, what they look like as waves, how they are heard. It is almost like a science of sound, closer to physics and biology.

Phonology, on the other hand, is concerned with how sounds function and pattern within a specific language — which sounds count as meaningfully different in a language, which ones can follow each other, and how sound systems are organised.

Here is a simple way to remember the difference:

Phonetics asks: "What is this sound, physically?"
Phonology asks: "What role does this sound play in this language?"

For example, in English, the "l" sound in light and the "l" sound in full are actually physically slightly different sounds. Phonetics notices and describes both. But phonology says: in English, this difference does not change the meaning of any word, so both are treated as the same unit. In some other languages, the same difference would change a word's meaning — and phonology of that language would treat them as two separate units.

Two key terms you will often encounter in phonetics:

A phone is any single, distinct speech sound — just a sound, studied on its own, without thinking about meaning or language rules. Phonetics deals with phones.

A phoneme is a sound unit that is meaningful within a specific language — one that, if changed, would change or destroy the meaning of a word. Phonology deals with phonemes.

Example: Change the first sound of the word cat from "k" to "b" and you get bat — a completely different word. So "k" and "b" are different phonemes in English. They matter.

Because different languages spell the same sounds differently (the "sh" sound in English is written ⟨sh⟩, but in French it is ⟨ch⟩, and in German ⟨sch⟩), phoneticians needed a universal writing system for sounds — one symbol for each sound, regardless of which language it appears in.

That system is the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA). It is a set of symbols where each symbol represents exactly one sound, consistently, across all languages. So the "sh" sound in all three languages above is written as a single IPA symbol: /ʃ/. If you have ever seen a dictionary showing the pronunciation of a word using strange-looking symbols between slashes or square brackets, you were looking at IPA.

Phonetics relies heavily on the IPA to record and communicate about sounds precisely.
Where is phonetics used in real life?

Phonetics is not just an academic subject. It has direct, practical applications:

  • Language learning and teaching — Understanding phonetics helps teachers explain why learners make certain pronunciation mistakes, and helps learners consciously correct them. A French speaker learning English who struggles with "th" sounds can benefit from a phonetic explanation of exactly how to position the tongue.
  • Speech therapy — Speech-language pathologists use phonetics to diagnose and treat difficulties with speech sounds in children and adults — stuttering, lisps, articulation disorders, and so on.
  • Linguistics and language documentation — When researchers study or record a new or endangered language, phonetics gives them the tools to accurately describe the sounds of that language.
  • Voice technology — Speech recognition systems (like the ones in virtual assistants), text-to-speech engines, and voice translation tools all depend on phonetic knowledge to work.
  • Forensic linguistics — Phonetic analysis can be used to study recorded voices — for example, to help identify a speaker in a legal case.
  • Dialect and accent studies — Phoneticians can analyse the exact sound differences between regional accents or dialects of a language.

Phonetics is the scientific, systematic study of human speech sounds. It examines how sounds are physically produced by the body (articulatory phonetics), what they look like as travelling sound waves (acoustic phonetics), and how they are heard and processed by the listener (auditory phonetics). It is distinct from phonology, which is concerned with how sounds function within a particular language's system. Phonetics provides the foundational, precise, science-based understanding of speech that underlies language teaching, speech therapy, voice technology, and linguistics as a whole.
